name: Civil rights movement
title: The story of the civil rights movement

text: In the southern United States, laws called Jim Crow laws kept Black people apart in schools, trains, parks and hospitals.
Most Black people there were also stopped from voting, through unfair taxes, tests and threats.
src: Jim Crow laws segregated schools, trains, streetcars, parks and hospitals
Poll taxes, literacy tests, all-white primaries and intimidation removed most Black voters from the rolls

text: In 1955 Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger.
Months earlier, a fifteen-year-old girl, Claudette Colvin, had been arrested for keeping her seat too.
src: On 1 December 1955 Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger
in March 1955, nine months before her arrest, the fifteen-year-old Claudette Colvin was arrested for keeping her seat on a Montgomery bus

text: Black people in Montgomery stopped riding the buses for 381 days, until the buses were opened to everyone.
src: Black residents, three-quarters of the riders, boycotted the buses for 381 days, until the Supreme Court’s ruling in Browder v. Gayle desegregated them
the domestic workers who walked to work in Montgomery

text: Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist minister, became the movement's best-known voice.
He and many others protested without violence, accepting arrest without striking back.
src: Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968), a Baptist minister with a doctorate from Boston University, became the movement’s best-known voice
Most of its leaders shared a faith in non-violent direct action / by accepting arrest and violence without striking back

text: In 1963 about 250,000 people joined the March on Washington, where King spoke of his dream.
Peaceful marchers often met violence, and pictures of it helped persuade Congress to change the laws.
src: On 28 August some 250,000 people joined the March on Washington / 1963: The Birmingham campaign and the March on Washington, where King speaks of his dream
Non-violent campaigns from Montgomery to Selma met violent resistance, and the images of that violence helped persuade Congress

text: New laws in 1964 and 1965 ended legal segregation and most barriers to Black voting in the South.
King was killed in 1968, but the movement inspired people fighting for equal rights around the world.
src: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 ended legal segregation and most barriers to Black voting in the South
1968: Martin Luther King Jr. is assassinated in Memphis / inspired movements for equal rights across the world
